newsitem.title: UK: Glaxo Wellcome R&D update-other highlights.
newsitem.headline: Glaxo Wellcome R&D update-other highlights.

text.p: Among other areas of the drugs pipeline highlighted by Glaxo Wellcome Plc in its research and development update on Friday were:

ANTIBIOTICS - The company said it was developing two new antibiotics targeted at respiratory infections. The first, Grepafloxacin, which is filed for regulatory approval, has the potential to overcome resistance to existing treatments, the company said. The second, Sanfetrinem, also shows ability to overcome organisms that are resistant to existing drugs.

DIABETES - The company said it had developed Romozin, a drug to treat type II diabetes, which affects up to 90 percent of all diabetics, including 30 million people in Europe. "Its prevalence is expected to double over the next ten years," said Glaxo Wellcome.

It said it was waiting for European approval of Romozin, which it described as "a novel treatment which attacks the underlying disease by reversing insulin resistance, allowing patients to reduce or discontinue insulin therapy."

IRRITABLE BOWEL SYNDROME (IBS) - The company said Phase II trials involving Glaxo Wellcome's Alosetron had shown it to be effective in meeting the primary unmet medical need resulting from IBS, relief of abdominal pain. A Phase III clinical trial is planned for later this year with the first regulatory filings planned for 1999.

ENLARGED PROSTATE - Glaxo Wellcome said a new drug for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH), which affects half of men over 50, had been shown in Phase II trials to decrease the prostate size and improve symptoms. The first regulatory submissions for the drug, GI198745, are intended for 1999 after a Phase III clinical trial programme due to commence this year.

SEPTIC SHOCK - It said Phase II trials of its septic shock drug 546C88 significantly reduced patients' production of nitric oxide, which it said had a key role in the condition, which kills 50 percent of sufferers. A Phase III clinical trial programme is underway, with the first regulatory submissions likely in 2001.

STROKE - The company said its new compound, GV150526, reduced the damaging effects of stroke on the brain. "Significantly this novel product can be administered up to 8-12 hours after the stroke and there is no requirement for neuroradiology prior to its use," it said.
Phase III clinical trials are due to start this year, with regulatory filings expected to take place in the year 2000, Glaxo Wellcome said.
